DOCKER COMPOSE SECURITY CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

What is your docker-compose.yml handing to the host?

One privileged: true, a mounted docker.sock, network_mode: host or a database published on 0.0.0.0 can turn a bug in one container into control of the machine. Paste your own compose file below and this page lists each risky setting with its line, the risk, and the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own. It is a heuristic line scan, not a security audit.

1. Paste your compose file

Paste the contents of your own docker-compose.yml or compose.yaml. Add more blocks for override files. Give each block its real file name so findings point at the right file.

Paste at least one compose file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeRiskFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                       # scan compose files under the current directory
python3 check.py compose.yaml deploy/  # scan specific files or directories
python3 check.py --format json         # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk        # exit 2 on any medium or high finding

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. It finds docker-compose*.yml and compose*.yaml files and skips node_modules, vendor, .git and build folders.

Common questions

What makes a docker-compose.yml risky?

Settings that hand a container the host or leak a credential: privileged: true, the Docker socket mounted in, network_mode: host, cap_add ALL or SYS_ADMIN, host paths such as / or /etc bind-mounted, seccomp or AppArmor switched off, shared host pid or ipc namespaces, a database port published on every interface, and passwords written as literal environment values. Any one of them can turn a bug in one container into control of the machine.

Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock dangerous?

Anything that can talk to the Docker socket can start a new privileged container with the host filesystem mounted, which is root on the host. Mounting it read-only does not help, because the API is still fully usable. If a tool needs Docker, put a socket proxy that allows only the endpoints it needs in front of it.

Why does a database port published on 0.0.0.0 matter?

A ports entry such as "5432:5432" binds the host's every interface, so the database is reachable from the whole network, and Docker's own firewall rules bypass ufw and similar tools. Bind it to loopback with "127.0.0.1:5432:5432", or publish nothing and let other services reach it by service name.

Does this tool send my compose file anywhere?

No. It makes no network calls at all. The file you paste is scanned in this page and never leaves your device, and secret values are never printed in the results.

Does a clean scan mean my stack is safe?

No. This is a heuristic line scan, not a security audit. It reads only the patterns listed here, does not expand anchors, extends, includes or variables, and cannot judge your images, host, firewall or secrets handling. Have a qualified person review anything that protects valuable data.

More: what makes a docker-compose.yml risky, and how do you fix each setting?

what-is-docker-compose-security.html.text:
← Docker Compose Security Check

docker-compose security: privileged, docker.sock, exposed ports and how to fix each

A Compose file decides how much of the host each container can touch. Most compose-related incidents are not clever exploits. They are one line that removed a boundary, such as a database published on every interface or a credential committed in plain text.

# hands the host to the container
services:
  web:
    privileged: true
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock

# narrow, loopback-only, pinned
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:5432:5432"]
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password

The thirteen patterns a line scan can find

  • compose-privileged — privileged: true. Fix: delete it; grant one device or capability instead.
  • compose-docker-socket — /var/run/docker.sock mounted. Root on the host, even with :ro. Fix: remove it or use a socket proxy.
  • compose-host-network — network_mode: host. Fix: publish only the ports you need.
  • compose-dangerous-capability — cap_add: [ALL] or SYS_ADMIN. Fix: cap_drop: [ALL] and add back one narrow capability.
  • compose-exposed-database-port — 5432, 3306, 6379, 27017 or 9200 published without a loopback address. Fix: "127.0.0.1:5432:5432" or no ports:.
  • compose-literal-secret — a PASSWORD, SECRET, TOKEN or API_KEY set to a literal in environment:. Fix: .env outside version control or Docker secrets, then rotate. The tool never prints the value.
  • compose-sensitive-host-mount — host path /, /etc, /root, /boot, /proc or /sys mounted. Fix: mount one directory, read-only when possible.
  • compose-security-opt-unconfined — seccomp:unconfined, apparmor:unconfined or label:disable. Fix: delete it so Docker's default profiles apply.
  • compose-host-namespace — pid: host or ipc: host. Fix: use the private default.
  • compose-runs-as-root — user: root, 0 or 0:0. Fix: user: "1000:1000". Medium.
  • compose-image-latest — an image with no tag or :latest. Fix: pin a version or digest. Medium.
  • compose-no-restart — no restart policy. Fix: restart: unless-stopped. Low.
  • compose-no-healthcheck — no healthcheck. Fix: add one so dependents can wait on service_healthy. Low.

Is privileged: true ever needed in docker compose?

Rarely. It disables most of the isolation Docker provides, so a compromised container can load kernel modules, read host devices and escape to the host. Almost every real need is narrower: map one device with devices:, or add one capability such as NET_ADMIN with cap_add, and keep privileged off.

Is mounting docker.sock into a container safe?

No. The Docker API is root on the host: a container that can reach it can start another container with the host filesystem mounted. A :ro suffix does not restrict the API. If a dashboard or CI agent needs it, use a socket proxy that exposes only the read-only endpoints required.

How do I stop a published database port being reachable from the internet?

Bind it to loopback in ports: with "127.0.0.1:5432:5432", or remove ports: entirely, since other services on the same Compose network reach it by service name. Remember Docker writes its own firewall rules, so a host firewall such as ufw does not block a port you published on 0.0.0.0.

Check your own compose file

Paste your compose file into Docker Compose Security Check to see every finding with its line, risk and fix, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status on any medium or high finding, so you can wire it into your own CI. Expect some findings to be deliberate (a monitoring agent may truly need the socket); review each one.

Have a qualified person review anything that protects valuable data.
